newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian children call for action on sex abuse.
newsitem.headline: Belgian children call for action on sex abuse.

text.p: Belgium's painful soul-searching over how it allowed a fatal child sex-abuse racket to develop within its borders took a new turn on Sunday, with abused children addressing an international conference of experts.
Belgian King Albert and Queen Paola, along with Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene and other senior politicians, listened as children themselves called their elders to take action against exploitation.

Cedric, a teenager sexually abused by one of his schoolteachers, spoke of his betrayal, hatred and subsequent aggression towards all adults, punctuating the account with rythmic cadenzas on his African tom-tom drum.
"There is no penalty strong enough to punish the crime that is paedophilia," he told the assembled politicians and royalty.
"And so for once honourable ministers, for once, hit hard with your actions," he urged.
While Cedric's alleged abuser now faces criminal proceedings, others remain at large, their victims unidentified and those victims' families unconsoled.
Five mothers, all with missing children, urged delegates to join them in forging an international network to fight the sexual exploitation of minors.
Sunday's event, the start of a four-day forum called "The children are calling", is only the latest response to last year's grisly saga of paedophilia and murder in Belgium.

Delegates are due to debate proposals from the National Commission against the Sexual Exploitation of Children, set up on August 30 barely two weeks after the rescue of two sexually abused young girls from a makeshift dungeon in the house of convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux.

Within days, police dug up the bodies of two eight-year-old girls in another of his houses nearby and, less than a week later, unearthed the bodies of two teenage girls in the grounds of another property linked to the same man.
Dutroux has been charged with the murder of all four.
Commission president Geert Cappelaere opened proceedings with a reminder that while it had been Belgium's sad lot to witness these children's murders, the problem was a global one.

"While we must reflect why precisely this happened in our country, it would be wrong to reduce this problem to the level of a national phenomenon. Children are victims of injustices throughout the entire world," he said.
